questions.stem: Which statement about Windows Defender Firewall is NOT true?

options.text: It blocks all outbound traffic by default
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: outbound traffic is allowed by default.

options.text: It has separate Domain, Private, and Public profiles
options.rationale: True.

options.text: Inbound traffic is blocked unless a rule allows it
options.rationale: True.

options.text: The active profile depends on the network location
options.rationale: True.

questions.explanation: Windows Defender Firewall is a built-in host-based firewall with Domain, Private, and Public profiles. Inbound is blocked unless allowed; outbound is allowed by default.
questions.discriminator_tested: Inbound blocked by default; outbound allowed by default.

questions.stem: Endpoint monitoring flags powershell.exe on an accounting PC downloading and running code from the internet at 3 a.m. No new program was installed. What technique does this most likely show?

options.text: Living off the land: an attacker misusing a built-in scripting tool
options.rationale: Correct: legitimate built-in tools let attackers avoid installing anything new.

options.text: Adware bundled with a free program
options.rationale: No program was installed, and nothing involves ads.

options.text: A hardware fault in the network card
options.rationale: Hardware faults don't download and run code.

options.text: A failed firmware update
options.rationale: Firmware updates don't run code through PowerShell.

questions.explanation: Scripting tools such as PowerShell, batch, VBScript, and Python automate admin tasks, and attackers abuse the same built-in tools, known as 'living off the land'.
questions.discriminator_tested: Attackers use the same scripting tools as admins.

questions.stem: Which practice is NOT a recommended Windows security consideration?

options.text: Leaving unused services running in case they are needed later
options.rationale: Correct choice: every unused service adds attack surface.

options.text: Encrypting disks with BitLocker
options.rationale: Recommended.

options.text: Using a standard user account for daily work
options.rationale: Recommended.

options.text: Running antimalware
options.rationale: Recommended.

questions.explanation: Windows hardening means daily use as a standard user, disabling unused accounts and services, running antimalware, and using BitLocker, to reduce the attack surface with layered controls.
questions.discriminator_tested: Hardening reduces attack surface.

questions.stem: Which two statements about NTFS permissions are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: Permissions from different groups are cumulative
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: They apply to both local and network access
options.rationale: Correct: NTFS permissions are always checked.

options.text: They apply only to network access
options.rationale: That describes share permissions.

options.text: An Allow entry always overrides a Deny entry
options.rationale: Deny overrides Allow (and an explicit entry beats an inherited one).

options.text: Read includes the right to take ownership
options.rationale: Take ownership is part of Full control.

questions.explanation: NTFS permissions apply to both local and network access, are cumulative across groups, and Deny overrides Allow. Full control adds change permissions and take ownership on top of Modify.
questions.discriminator_tested: NTFS: local and network, cumulative, Deny overrides Allow.

questions.stem: A folder's share permissions give Everyone Read. Its NTFS permissions give a user Modify. That user logs on at the server's own console and tries to edit a file in the folder. Is the edit allowed?

options.text: Yes: locally only NTFS permissions apply, so the user has Modify
options.rationale: Correct: share permissions don't affect local access.

options.text: No: the share's Read permission restricts the user
options.rationale: Share permissions apply only over the network.

options.text: No: locally, neither set of permissions applies
options.rationale: NTFS still applies locally.

options.text: Only if the share permission is raised to Change
options.rationale: The share permission doesn't matter for local access.

questions.explanation: For local permissions (a user at the machine itself), only NTFS permissions apply and share permissions are ignored. Over the network, the more restrictive of the two would win.
questions.discriminator_tested: Locally, only NTFS applies.

questions.stem: Which two statements about share permissions are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: They apply only to access over the network
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Combined with NTFS permissions, the more restrictive of the two is the effective access
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: They also apply to users logged on locally
options.rationale: Only NTFS applies locally.

options.text: They include Modify and List folder contents
options.rationale: Those are NTFS permissions; share permissions are Read, Change, and Full Control.

options.text: Full Control at the share overrides an NTFS Deny
options.rationale: The more restrictive layer still wins, so the NTFS Deny holds.

questions.explanation: Share permissions (Read, Change, Full Control) apply only to network access. When combined with NTFS, the more restrictive of the two determines effective access.
questions.discriminator_tested: Share permissions: network only; the more restrictive of share and NTFS wins.

questions.stem: Under file permission inheritance logic, which order of precedence is correct for NTFS permission entries, from strongest to weakest?

options.text: Explicit Deny, explicit Allow, inherited Deny, inherited Allow
options.rationale: Correct: explicit entries beat inherited ones, and Deny beats Allow at the same level.

options.text: Inherited Deny, explicit Allow, explicit Deny, inherited Allow
options.rationale: An explicit Allow beats an inherited Deny, and an explicit Deny beats both.

options.text: Explicit Allow, explicit Deny, inherited Allow, inherited Deny
options.rationale: At the same level, Deny comes before Allow.

options.text: Inherited Allow, inherited Deny, explicit Allow, explicit Deny
options.rationale: Explicit entries take precedence over inherited ones.

questions.explanation: Child objects inherit permissions by default. Precedence is explicit Deny, then explicit Allow, then inherited Deny, then inherited Allow, so an explicit Allow can override an inherited Deny.
questions.discriminator_tested: Explicit Deny > explicit Allow > inherited Deny > inherited Allow.

questions.stem: Which two statements about shared files and folders on Windows are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: They are published over SMB on TCP 445
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: A share name ending in $ only hides it from browsing
options.rationale: Correct: it can still be reached by name.

options.text: A share name ending in $ stops anyone from connecting
options.rationale: Anyone who knows the name and has permission can connect.

options.text: Shares are accessed over Telnet on TCP 23
options.rationale: File sharing uses SMB on TCP 445.

options.text: Administrative shares such as C$ are encrypted by default
options.rationale: The $ hides the share; it doesn't encrypt it.

questions.explanation: Shared folders are published over SMB (TCP 445). Hidden and administrative shares end in $ (such as C$ and ADMIN$), and the $ only hides a share from browsing; it doesn't secure it.
questions.discriminator_tested: SMB on TCP 445; $ hides but doesn't secure.

questions.stem: Which threat does User Account Control (UAC) most directly reduce?

options.text: Malware silently gaining administrative rights when an administrator runs it
options.rationale: Correct: administrators run with a standard token until they approve an elevation.

options.text: Phishing emails reaching the inbox
options.rationale: UAC doesn't filter email.

options.text: A SYN flood against a web server
options.rationale: That is a network attack, unrelated to local elevation.

options.text: Physical theft of the laptop
options.rationale: Disk encryption addresses that.

questions.explanation: UAC prompts before actions that need administrative rights. Because administrators run with a standard token until they elevate, malware can't silently gain admin rights.
questions.discriminator_tested: UAC stops malware from silently gaining admin rights.

questions.stem: A company with 2,000 Windows PCs wants to approve and schedule Windows Updates centrally, instead of letting each PC update on its own. What should it use?

options.text: WSUS or Intune
options.rationale: Correct: both centralize control over Windows Update.

options.text: The Mac App Store
options.rationale: That distributes macOS apps.

options.text: apt
options.rationale: apt is a Linux package manager.

options.text: Event Viewer
options.rationale: Event Viewer reads logs; it doesn't manage updates.

questions.explanation: Windows Update delivers security, quality, and feature updates, and WSUS or Intune centralize control: approving, scheduling, and reporting across many PCs.
questions.discriminator_tested: WSUS or Intune centralize Windows Updates.

questions.stem: On a Windows PC, which two items typically need their own patching process outside Windows Update? (Choose two.)

options.text: A third-party web browser
options.rationale: Correct: third-party apps update themselves or through their vendor.

options.text: A third-party PDF reader
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: The Windows kernel
options.rationale: The kernel is patched through Windows Update.

options.text: The built-in Windows Defender Firewall
options.rationale: Built-in Windows components are patched through Windows Update.

options.text: The monthly Windows cumulative security update
options.rationale: That is delivered by Windows Update.

questions.explanation: Application patching is its own process: patching the OS does not patch most third-party applications, such as browsers, PDF readers, and runtimes.
questions.discriminator_tested: OS patches don't cover most third-party apps.

questions.stem: Which statement about device drivers on Windows is NOT true?

options.text: 64-bit Windows loads unsigned kernel-mode drivers by default
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: 64-bit Windows requires signed kernel drivers.

options.text: Drivers run in kernel mode
options.rationale: True.

options.text: Rolling back a driver restores the previous version
options.rationale: True.

options.text: A driver is OS-side software that lets the OS talk to hardware
options.rationale: True.

questions.explanation: Device drivers are OS-side software running in kernel mode. 64-bit Windows requires signed kernel drivers, and rollback restores the prior driver. Firmware, by contrast, is code stored on the device.
questions.discriminator_tested: 64-bit Windows requires signed kernel drivers.

questions.stem: When a user opens an app downloaded from a website, macOS warns that it cannot be opened because the developer cannot be verified. Which feature produced this warning, and why?

options.text: Gatekeeper, because the app isn't from an identified or notarized developer
options.rationale: Correct: Gatekeeper checks apps from outside the store.

options.text: The Mac App Store review, because Apple rejected the app
options.rationale: The app didn't come through the store at all.

options.text: The application firewall, because the app tried to use the network
options.rationale: The firewall controls network connections, not whether an app may open.

options.text: UAC, because the app needs administrator rights
options.rationale: UAC is a Windows feature.

questions.explanation: The Mac App Store is Apple's reviewed, sandboxed source. Gatekeeper controls apps from outside the store, allowing identified or notarized developers and warning about the rest.
questions.discriminator_tested: Gatekeeper covers apps from outside the store.

questions.stem: Which two pairings of an operating system with its system updates tool are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: Ubuntu: apt
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Fedora: dnf
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: macOS: apt
options.rationale: macOS updates come from Apple's Software Update.

options.text: Red Hat: Windows Update
options.rationale: Red Hat uses dnf or yum.

options.text: Debian: the Mac App Store
options.rationale: Debian uses apt.

questions.explanation: System updates: macOS uses Software Update; Linux uses its package manager (apt on Debian and Ubuntu, dnf or yum on Red Hat and Fedora), which updates the OS and repo-installed apps together.
questions.discriminator_tested: apt = Debian/Ubuntu; dnf/yum = Red Hat/Fedora; macOS updates come from Apple.

questions.stem: Which step is NOT part of a sound patch management process?

options.text: Deploying every patch straight to all production systems, without testing
options.rationale: Correct choice: patches are tested before production, with a rollback plan.

options.text: Keeping an inventory of systems and software
options.rationale: A real step: you can't patch what you don't know about.

options.text: Testing patches before broad deployment
options.rationale: A real step.

options.text: Documenting what was deployed and verified
options.rationale: A real step.

questions.explanation: Patch management is an ongoing process: inventory, identify, evaluate and test, approve, deploy, verify, and document. It tests before production and keeps a rollback plan.
questions.discriminator_tested: Test before production; patching is a managed process.

questions.stem: An Ubuntu server should accept SSH (TCP 22) only from the admin subnet and refuse other inbound connections. Which firewall approach fits?

options.text: Use ufw, a front-end to netfilter, to allow TCP 22 from the admin subnet and deny other inbound traffic
options.rationale: Correct: Linux firewall rules are port- and address-based.

options.text: Turn on the macOS application firewall
options.rationale: That is a macOS feature.

options.text: Switch Windows Defender Firewall to the Public profile
options.rationale: That is a Windows feature.

options.text: Run chmod 700 on the SSH program
options.rationale: File permissions don't filter network connections.

questions.explanation: Linux firewalls use netfilter, managed through iptables/nftables or front-ends such as ufw and firewalld, with port- and address-based rules. macOS uses a per-application firewall.
questions.discriminator_tested: Linux firewall rules are port/address-based; ufw is a front-end.

questions.stem: An administrator runs 'chmod 754 deploy.sh' on a Linux system. Which two statements about the resulting permissions are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: The owner can read, write, and execute
options.rationale: Correct: 7 = 4 + 2 + 1.

options.text: The group can read and execute
options.rationale: Correct: 5 = 4 + 1.

options.text: Others can read, write, and execute
options.rationale: Others get 4, which is read only.

options.text: The group can write
options.rationale: 5 does not include write (2).

options.text: Others have no access at all
options.rationale: Others get read (4).

questions.explanation: Linux/UNIX permissions use three digits for owner, group, and others, with read = 4, write = 2, and execute = 1. 754 means rwx for the owner, r-x for the group, and r-- for others.
questions.discriminator_tested: Three digits = owner, group, others; r=4, w=2, x=1.

questions.stem: Which statement about driver and firmware updates is NOT true?

options.text: Interrupting a firmware update is harmless, because the device simply retries at next boot
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is false: an interrupted firmware update can brick the device.

options.text: They fix bugs and vulnerabilities
options.rationale: True.

options.text: They should come from the vendor and be checked for integrity
options.rationale: True.

options.text: They include BIOS/UEFI, NIC, and storage firmware
options.rationale: True.

questions.explanation: Driver and firmware updates fix bugs and vulnerabilities. Get them from the vendor and verify their integrity, because an interrupted or bad firmware update can brick the device.
questions.discriminator_tested: An interrupted firmware update can brick the device.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly orders an operating system's life cycle?

options.text: Release, mainstream support, extended support, end of support
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Release, end of support, mainstream support, extended support
options.rationale: End of support comes last.

options.text: Extended support, release, mainstream support, end of support
options.rationale: Extended support follows mainstream support.

options.text: Mainstream support, extended support, release, end of support
options.rationale: Release comes first.

questions.explanation: The OS life cycle runs release, mainstream support, extended support, then end of support. After end of support there are no security patches unless a paid Extended Security Updates program covers the device; Windows 10, for example, ended support on October 14, 2025.
questions.discriminator_tested: After end of support (outside paid ESU) there are no security patches.

questions.stem: Which two pairings of an Event Viewer log with what it records are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: Security: logons and audited actions
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: System: OS components and drivers
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Application: logon attempts
options.rationale: Logons are recorded in the Security log.

options.text: Security: driver load failures
options.rationale: Driver events are recorded in the System log.

options.text: System: errors from programs users installed
options.rationale: Program events are recorded in the Application log.

questions.explanation: In Event Viewer, the Security log holds logons and audited actions, the System log holds OS components and drivers, and the Application log holds programs. Levels are Critical, Error, Warning, and Information.
questions.discriminator_tested: Security = logons and audits; System = OS and drivers; Application = programs.

questions.stem: On a Linux server, which component records security-relevant actions, such as file access and privilege use, according to configured rules?

options.text: auditd
options.rationale: Correct: it produces Linux audit logs.

options.text: ufw
options.rationale: ufw manages firewall rules.

options.text: apt
options.rationale: apt installs and updates packages.

options.text: chmod
options.rationale: chmod changes permissions; it doesn't record actions.

questions.explanation: Audit logs record security-relevant actions (who, what, when, from where). They are enabled by audit policy on Windows or by auditd on Linux, and they must be protected from tampering.
questions.discriminator_tested: Audit logs come from audit policy on Windows and auditd on Linux.

questions.stem: Logs from branch firewalls cross an untrusted WAN to a central collector. Losing log messages or exposing their contents is unacceptable. Which transport fits?

options.text: Syslog over TLS (TCP 6514)
options.rationale: Correct: TCP adds reliability, and TLS adds confidentiality.

options.text: Default syslog on UDP 514
options.rationale: UDP 514 is cleartext and unreliable.

options.text: SNMPv2c traps
options.rationale: Traps are alerts, not log streams, and v2c is cleartext.

options.text: TFTP
options.rationale: TFTP is unauthenticated file transfer.

questions.explanation: Syslog by default uses UDP 514, which is cleartext and unreliable. Syslog over TCP adds reliability, and over TLS (6514) adds security.
questions.discriminator_tested: UDP 514 is cleartext and unreliable; TLS on 6514 adds security.

questions.stem: A company sends all device logs to a syslog collector. Management assumes it will be alerted automatically when a brute force attack shows up across the firewall, server, and VPN logs together. What is missing?

options.text: A SIEM to correlate events across sources and raise alerts; a collector only stores the logs
options.rationale: Correct: storage is not analysis.

options.text: More disk space on the collector
options.rationale: Storage space doesn't create alerts.

options.text: Switching syslog to UDP 514
options.rationale: The transport doesn't add correlation.

options.text: Turning on Event Viewer on the routers
options.rationale: Event Viewer is a Windows log viewer and doesn't correlate.

questions.explanation: A syslog collector is a central server that receives and keeps syslog from many devices. Correlating events across sources and alerting is the job of a SIEM.
questions.discriminator_tested: A collector stores logs; it doesn't correlate them.

questions.stem:
A router logs:

%SEC-6-IPACCESSLOGP: list 101 denied tcp 10.1.1.5(51544) -> 10.2.2.2(23), 1 packet

Which statement about this syslog message is correct?

options.text: SEC is the facility, 6 is the severity (Informational), and IPACCESSLOGP is the mnemonic
options.rationale: Correct: the format is %FACILITY-SEVERITY-MNEMONIC.

options.text: 6 is the ACL number
options.rationale: The ACL number, 101, appears in the description.

options.text: SEC is the severity level
options.rationale: SEC is the facility; the severity is the number.

options.text: 6 means Emergency
options.rationale: Emergency is 0; 6 is Informational.

questions.explanation: Cisco syslog messages use the format %FACILITY-SEVERITY-MNEMONIC: description. The number in the middle is the severity level, here 6 (Informational).
questions.discriminator_tested: The number in the middle is the severity.

questions.stem: Which pairing of a logging severity level with its name is NOT correct?

options.text: 0: Debugging
options.rationale: Correct choice because it is wrong: 0 is Emergency, and Debugging is 7.

options.text: 3: Error
options.rationale: Correct pairing.

options.text: 4: Warning
options.rationale: Correct pairing.

options.text: 6: Informational
options.rationale: Correct pairing.

questions.explanation: Severity levels are 0 Emergency, 1 Alert, 2 Critical, 3 Error, 4 Warning, 5 Notification, 6 Informational, 7 Debugging. A lower number is more severe.
questions.discriminator_tested: Lower number = more severe; 0 is Emergency, 7 is Debugging.

questions.stem: Why does identifying anomalies in logs depend on having a baseline?

options.text: Without knowing what normal activity looks like, you can't tell which events are unusual
options.rationale: Correct: an anomaly is a deviation from a known normal.

options.text: Baselines encrypt the logs
options.rationale: A baseline describes normal behavior; it doesn't encrypt anything.

options.text: Baselines delete old logs to save space
options.rationale: Retention is a separate setting.

options.text: Anomaly detection only matches known signatures
options.rationale: Matching known patterns is signature-based detection.

questions.explanation: Identifying anomalies means comparing log activity with a baseline, for example off-hours logons, repeated failed logons, or new admin accounts. Without a baseline, unusual can't be told from normal.
questions.discriminator_tested: An anomaly needs a baseline.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a typical SIEM function?

options.text: Blocking packets inline at the network edge
options.rationale: Correct choice: inline blocking is done by an IPS or firewall.

options.text: Aggregating logs from many sources
options.rationale: A SIEM function.

options.text: Correlating events across sources
options.rationale: A SIEM function: the key one.

options.text: Alerts and dashboards
options.rationale: A SIEM function.

questions.explanation: A SIEM aggregates, normalizes, and correlates logs from many sources, with alerts, dashboards, and retention. It analyzes events; it doesn't sit inline blocking traffic.
questions.discriminator_tested: A SIEM correlates logs across sources.
